column2: Why can conventional karyotyping miss small changes or some cell populations?
column3: Its resolution is limited, so most small copy changes and nucleotide variants are invisible, and cell culture can select against some cell populations.

column2: Why does a normal fluorescence in situ hybridisation result not exclude other chromosomal abnormalities?
column3: Labelled probes bind only selected DNA regions, so the assay sees only the targeted sequences.

column2: Which abnormalities does chromosomal microarray generally miss despite genome-wide coverage, and why?
column3: Because it measures copy number, it generally misses balanced rearrangements, many low-level mosaics, repeat expansions and small sequence variants.

column2: Why are PCR-based assays vulnerable to false or missing results?
column3: Their results depend on primer placement, making them vulnerable to allele dropout, contamination and unrecognised variation under primer-binding sites.

column2: Why does adequate mean sequencing depth not guarantee that a variant would be detected?
column3: Coverage is uneven: repeats, pseudogenes, high-GC regions, homologous genes and low-complexity sequence are difficult, so mean depth does not prove every base is adequately covered.

column2: What can long-read sequencing resolve that short-read sequencing struggles with?
column3: Long reads span larger structures, repeats, methylation and haplotypes, whereas short reads struggle to phase distant variants and resolve long repeats or rearrangements.

column2: Why can RNA sequencing of blood fail to show the consequence of a DNA variant?
column3: It depends on expression in the sampled tissue and on transcript stability; nonsense-mediated decay may erase the abnormal transcript, and blood may not show muscle- or brain-specific isoforms.

column2: Why may a predicted loss-of-function variant not actually cause disease?
column3: A stop near the gene end may escape decay, the exon may be alternatively skipped, a splice variant may preserve frame, or the gene may tolerate haploinsufficiency.

column2: Why does finding a variant in an unaffected relative weaken but not refute disease association?
column3: If penetrance is incomplete, carriers can remain unaffected, so an unaffected carrier does not disprove the association.

column2: Why should a variant of uncertain significance not drive irreversible predictive or surgical decisions?
column3: Its disease association is unresolved, and it can be reclassified as population data, family studies, functional evidence or disease knowledge grow, so patients need a plan for review.

column2: Why does variant allele fraction in tumour testing not simply indicate zygosity?
column3: It also reflects tumour purity, copy number, clonality and heterogeneity, and clonal haematopoiesis can contaminate blood or cell-free DNA and mimic tumour or germline findings.

column3: Placental mosaicism, maternal variants, vanished twin, malignancy and low fetal fraction affect results, and positive predictive value depends strongly on prior probability.

column2: How do analytical validity, clinical validity and clinical utility differ?
column3: Analytical validity asks whether the assay detects the variant accurately, clinical validity whether the variant predicts phenotype, and clinical utility whether the result improves decisions or outcomes.

column2: Why do underrepresented groups receive more uncertain genomic results?
column3: Bias enters through reference genomes, training data, variant databases and ancestry imbalance, so these groups get more uncertain results and lower risk-score accuracy.
